#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). The estimates from MARTS are released approximately ten business days after the end of the reference month and are revised one month later by estimates from the Monthly Retail Trade and Food Services Survey (MRTS). Estimates are summarized by industry classification based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey - General FAQs


Who uses the statistics produced from data collected in the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services (MARTS)?
  • The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses these data for the nation's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimates and in developing the national accounts' input-output tables.
  • The Bureau of Labor Statistics uses these data as input to its Producer Price Indices and in developing productivity measurements.
  • Trade and professional organizations use these data to analyze industry trends and benchmark their own statistical programs, develop forecasts, and evaluate regulatory requirements.
  • The media use these data for news reports and background information.
  • Private businesses use these data to measure market share, analyze business potential, and plan investments.
What are economic indicators?
Economic indicators are statistical figures, which are used to track the growth and decline of activity in specific segments of the economy over time. Additional economic indicators produced in other areas at the Census Bureau include Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders; U.S. International Trade; Labor Force; Income; Poverty; Government Budget and Debt; Plant and Equipment Expenditures; and Retail Sales.

What kinds of businesses are included in the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services (MARTS)?
MARTS covers firms classified in the Retail Trade and Food Services sectors as defined by the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). Retail Trade, as defined by NAICS sectors 44-45, includes establishments engaged in selling merchandise in small quantities to the general public, without transformation, and rendering services incidental to the sale of merchandise. Two principal types of establishments classified in retail trade can be distinguished-

1. Store retailers operate fixed point-of-sale locations, located and designed to attract a high volume of walk-in customers. They have extensive displays of merchandise, use mass-media advertising to attract customers and typically sell merchandise to the general public for personal or household use. Some store retailers also provide after-sales services, such as repair and installation; for example, new automobile dealers.

2. Nonstore retailers also serve the general public, but their retailing methods differ. Such methods include paper and electronic catalogs, door-to-door solicitation, in-home demonstration, "infomercials," selling from portable stalls or through vending machines.

Food services, as defined by NAICS subsector 722, include establishments that prepare meals, snacks, and beverages to customer order for immediate on-premises and off-premises consumption.

Are the statistics produced from the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services (MARTS) available at the state or other sub-national level?
No. MARTS is designed to produce statistics at the national level only. Statistics at the state level and other more detailed geographic levels for selected data items are produced every 5 years as part of the Economic Census. For more information, please see

Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey - Sample Revision FAQs


What is a sample revision and why is it necessary?
A sample revision is the process used to re-design and re-select the samples for many of the Census Bureau’s surveys of the retail, wholesale, and service industries. This process is performed to:
  • ensure each sample is representative of its target population
  • improve the efficiency of each sample
  • incorporate updates to the industry classification structure
  • expand industry coverage of the survey
  • update questions and instructions to obtain more accurate data
  • redistribute burden for small and medium size businesses
How often is a sample revision performed for the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey?
Sample revisions are performed approximately every two and a half to three years.

When were estimates from the new Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey sample released?
Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey estimates based on the new sample were released with the November 2022 Advance Monthly Sales for Retail Trade and Food Services Report on December 15th, 2022.

What is the size of the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey sample?
The size of the current Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey sample is approximately 4,800 employer firms. The size of the prior Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey sample was approximately 5,500 firms.

Are the estimates from different Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey samples comparable?
Yes. Estimates from different samples have been linked to be on a comparable basis.

What was the impact of adopting the 2012 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) definitions for the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey?
Effective with the Annual Revision release on May 25th, 2018, advance monthly retail estimates have been published on a 2012 NAICS basis. Time series affected by the definition changes were restated to the beginning of the time series. For a complete list of the series that were restated, please review our summary of NAICS restatement and publication table changes.

I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). The estimates from MARTS are released approximately ten business days after the end of the reference month and are revised one month later by estimates from the Monthly Retail Trade and Food Services Survey (MRTS). Estimates are summarized by industry classification based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS), U.S. Census Bureau: dataset report

## Summary

Your description is mostly accurate. A few details need correcting or adding:

- **The advance number gets revised more than once.** The next month's MRTS-based figure is only the first revision. There is a second monthly revision and then a yearly benchmark revision.
- **The series changed definition in April 2025.** Nonemployer businesses were removed from the entire history, and the industry codes moved to NAICS 2017.
- **Release timing was disrupted in 2025–26** by government funding lapses.

MARTS is the earliest broad monthly measure of U.S. consumer spending. It is a Principal Federal Economic Indicator, it feeds into GDP, and markets watch it closely. Its published reports go back to October 1953.

---

## 1. Checking your description

| Your statement | What I found |
|---|---|
| Title: "Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)" | **Partly right.** Census uses two names. The survey is the "Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS)." The published report is "Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services." Your title blends the two, and some Census FAQ pages do the same. The Census API dataset is "Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services" (`timeseries/eits/marts`). |
| Publisher: U.S. Census Bureau | **Correct.** The Census Bureau is part of the Department of Commerce. Census pages name the Retail Indicators Branch as the operating unit. |
| Early national estimates of total sales and month-to-month change | **Correct.** The survey covers only the national level; there are no state or local figures. Each release also gives year-over-year change and estimates by industry ("kind of business"). |
| Released about 10 business days after the month ends | **Roughly right.** Older Census documentation says "about 9 working days." Collection ends on the 6th business day, and the report usually comes out mid-month at 8:30 a.m. ET. Funding lapses in 2025–26 pushed some releases much later (section 4). |
| Revised one month later by the MRTS | **Incomplete.** Each release has three figures: an advance estimate for the latest month, a preliminary figure for the month before (from the larger MRTS), and a revised figure for the month before that. All months are then benchmarked again in the yearly revision each spring. |
| Summarized by NAICS | **Correct.** It covers Retail Trade (NAICS 44–45) and Food Services and Drinking Places (NAICS 722). Since April 2025 it uses NAICS 2017; from May 2018 it used NAICS 2012. |
| "Retail and food service establishments" | **Worth clarifying.** Reports come from companies or tax-ID units (EINs), not individual stores. Since April 2025 the estimates cover only businesses with paid employees. |

---

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Agency:** U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce.
- **Sister survey:** The Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) is the larger survey MARTS samples from. MRTS also produces inventory data and the quarterly e-commerce report.
- **Data collection:** Historically handled through the Census Bureau's National Processing Center in Jeffersonville, Indiana. Responses now come in online or by phone.
- **Paperwork approval:** MARTS had its own OMB control number, 0607-0104. The current active approval appears to cover both surveys under 0607-0717, "Monthly Retail Surveys" (ICR 202511-0607-002).

## 3. Legal authority

- **Authority to collect:** Title 13, U.S. Code, Sections 131 and 182, as cited in the OMB approval. Section 182 lets Census run surveys between the five-yearly economic censuses.
- **Answering is voluntary.** Census documentation says the survey is authorized under Title 13 "and provides for voluntary responses." This matters for how reliable the survey stays over time (section 9).
- **Confidentiality:** Title 13, Section 9 says responses can be used only for statistics, and no published figure may identify a business. Under the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015, the systems that transmit responses are screened for cybersecurity risks.
- **Principal Federal Economic Indicator status:** Census calls MARTS "a designated principal economic indicator." OMB Statistical Policy Directives No. 3 and No. 4 apply. They require release on a pre-announced schedule, rules against early access, and separation of the release from political commentary.
- **Copyright:** As a work of the federal government it is public domain (17 U.S.C. §105), so it can be reused freely.

## 4. History and timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **Oct 1953** | First advance report in Census's online archive. PDFs of the old press releases are posted. |
| 1954–1991 | Archive gaps: no releases for May 1954, Jan 1956, Aug 1956, Dec 1958, Jan 1970, Dec 1973 and Aug 1991. |
| **Mar 1970 – Jan 1972** | Advance retail sales were **not produced at all**, a real break in the series. |
| Before ~2001 | The series used the older SIC industry codes. |
| ~2001 | Moved to NAICS, and food services became part of the headline name. The current NAICS-based series starts in **January 1992**. ALFRED's archived versions start June 2001. |
| 2013 | New sample introduced, according to the OMB statement. |
| **May 25, 2018** | Moved to NAICS 2012, with the full history restated. |
| **Dec 15, 2022** | New sample introduced, starting with November 2022 data. It has about 4,800 firms, down from about 5,500. Census links each new sample to the old one so the figures stay comparable. |
| **Apr 25, 2025** | Yearly revision: moved to **NAICS 2017**, and **nonemployer businesses were removed** from the entire history to match the new Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES) and the Economic Census. |
| **Oct–Nov 2025** | Government shutdown. September 2025 data moved from Oct 16 to **Nov 25, 2025**, and later releases were squeezed together. |
| **Early 2026** | The January 2026 report came out on Mar 6, 2026. It noted another "recent lapse in federal funding" and listed the next release as "to be determined." |

A small inconsistency: Census's schedule page lists August 2026 data for Sept 16, 2026, but FRED/ALFRED and the Census time-series page show a Sept 28, 2026 release. Check the schedule again before relying on specific dates.

## 5. Methodology (for data scientists)

- **Sampling frame:** Units already in the MRTS sample. The MRTS sample is about 12,000–13,000 units, depending on which Census document you read.
- **Design:** About 4,800 units across 36 industry groups, each split by size. Large firms are always included ("certainty units"). Others are chosen with probability tied to their MRTS weight; weights run from 1 to about 1,000.
- **No new businesses are added** between redesigns. Instead the sample is rebuilt every 2½–3 years.
- **Collection:** Starts at the end of the reference month. Phone follow-up begins on business day 3, and collection closes on business day 6.
- **How the estimate is calculated:** For each detailed industry, Census takes firms that reported in both months and computes the ratio of this month's sales to last month's. That ratio is multiplied by last month's preliminary MRTS total. Broader totals are sums of the detailed industries.
  - Most non-responding firms are not imputed; a few very influential firms are estimated from their past results.
  - Because of this method, the advance estimate depends on the MRTS figure for the previous month.
- **Seasonal adjustment:** X-13ARIMA-SEATS using the X-11 method, updated every month with all available data. It adjusts for seasons, holidays and trading days, **but not for prices**, so the numbers are in current dollars.
- **Measuring uncertainty:** Each change comes with a 90% confidence interval. If the interval includes zero, the release marks the change with an asterisk, meaning it is not statistically different from zero.
  - Example, January 2026: sales were $733.5B, a change of −0.2% (±0.4%)*, so not significant.
  - Estimates are withheld ("S") if the coefficient of variation is above 30% or the response rate is below 50%.
- **What it does not include:** inventories (those come from MRTS), state or local figures (see the Economic Census), price-adjusted sales, and, since April 2025, businesses without employees.

## 6. Who uses it

- **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** consumer spending, GDP and the national accounts' input-output tables.
- **Bureau of Labor Statistics:** Producer Price Indexes and productivity measures.
- **Federal Reserve Board:** to anticipate economic trends and inform monetary policy.
- **Council of Economic Advisers and Treasury:** policy analysis. Treasury filed comments in the OMB approval process.
- **Financial markets:** the release can move markets. Analysts often watch the "control group" (sales excluding autos, gasoline, building materials and food services) as a proxy for goods spending in GDP. That grouping is an analyst convention, not an official Census aggregate.
- **Trade groups, businesses, market researchers:** market share, demand forecasting and benchmarking.
- **Media:** a monthly headline about the U.S. consumer.
- **Researchers:** business cycles, short-term "nowcasting," and checking private card-spending data against an official benchmark.

## 7. Benefits to the public

- It is the earliest broad official measure of consumer spending, which is about two-thirds of GDP.
- Policy decisions on interest rates, taxes and spending rely on timely, unbiased data.
- It is free, public-domain and published on a fixed schedule with equal access for everyone.
- It has published error ranges, unlike most private alternatives.
- It offers more than 70 years of history for long-run comparisons, with the gaps noted in section 4.
- It is a neutral reference point for checking private and alternative data sources.

## 8. Where to get it (for data librarians and preservationists)

| Resource | Location |
|---|---|
| Program home, methodology, FAQs | census.gov/retail (methodology: `/retail/marts/how_surveys_are_collected.html`) |
| Current report and time series (1992 to present, adjusted and unadjusted, seasonal factors) | census.gov/retail/sales.html; census.gov/econ/currentdata/?programCode=MARTS |
| Historical PDFs, 1953 onward | census.gov/retail/marts/historic_releases.html; files named `www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/advYYMM.pdf` (e.g., `adv2601.pdf`) |
| Historical release dates | `census.gov/retail/marts/www/MARTSreleasedates.xls` |
| API | `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/marts` (needs a free key). Variables include `category_code`, `data_type_code`, `seasonally_adj`, `cell_value`, `error_data`, `time`. |
| FRED | Series RSAFS (seasonally adjusted), RSAFSNA (not adjusted), and percent-change series; FRED release ID 9 |
| ALFRED | Archived past versions back to 2001, which is essential because Census overwrites revised figures |
| Yearly revision reports | census.gov/retail/mrts/historic_releases.html |

**Preservation points:**
1. **Census overwrites revised figures.** The current files show only the latest numbers, so the figures people actually saw on release day survive only in the PDF archive and ALFRED. Archive each release as published.
2. **The April 2025 restatement redefined the whole history.** Copies made before and after April 2025 are not comparable. Keep both, with notes.
3. **Watch for breaks:** the 1970–72 gap, the SIC-to-NAICS change, the NAICS 2012 and 2017 restatements, and sample redesigns in 2013 and 2022.
4. **Keep the documentation with the data:** methodology pages, the restatement summary (`/retail/mrts/www/NAICS_Restatement_Summary.pdf`), OMB supporting statements on reginfo.gov, and the release-date file.
5. Website reorganizations have broken URLs before, such as the old "briefroom" links. Capture pages with the Wayback Machine or a similar web archive.

## 9. Policy concerns (for advocates)

- **Voluntary response:** Falling response rates mean wider error ranges and possible bias. The OMB statements discuss studies of nonresponse bias.
- **Shrinking sample:** It went from about 5,000–5,500 firms to about 4,800 in 2022. That cuts the burden on businesses but also reduces precision.
- **Funding lapses:** The 2025 and early-2026 lapses delayed a Principal Federal Economic Indicator by weeks, leaving policymakers without data at important moments.
- **Definition changes:** Dropping nonemployers keeps the survey consistent with AIES, but it leaves out sole proprietors and gig sellers. Their share of activity matters for questions about small businesses and fairness.
- **Current dollars only:** Headline growth can reflect inflation, including tariff-driven price increases, rather than more goods sold. Users need price indexes to separate the two.
- **Wider statistical-system pressures:** Budgets, staffing and modernization (moving to AIES) all affect how long and how comparably this series can continue.

## 10. Related datasets

Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS); Quarterly E-Commerce Report; Annual Retail Trade Survey, now folded into AIES; Economic Census (state and local detail every 5 years); Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales; BEA Personal Consumption Expenditures; BLS Consumer Price Index (for adjusting sales for inflation).

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context

Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

# Risk assessment: Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS), October 2026

MARTS itself has not been cut. Its paperwork approval was renewed before it expired, its content is unchanged, and releases are back on schedule as of mid-2026. The main risks come from the Census Bureau around it: about 1,300–1,500 staff gone, a political appointee running the Bureau, a smaller budget request for the account that pays for current surveys, and repeated funding lapses that delayed releases.

---

### 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- The archive of release PDFs going back to October 1953 is still online; the March 2026 and August 2026 releases (`adv2603.pdf`, `marts_current.pdf`) were retrievable during this check.
- The time series from 1992 to the present is still on census.gov, the Census API (`timeseries/eits/marts`) and FRED. ALFRED keeps earlier versions back to 2001.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- The April 2025 revision removed nonemployer businesses from the entire history and moved it to the NAICS 2017 industry codes. The published history was redefined rather than deleted.
- The 2026 revision (released Sept 28, 2026) changed adjusted figures back to January 2015 and unadjusted figures back to January 2018. It also tied them to the 2023 and 2024 Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES), the annual survey that sets the yearly totals.
- Census overwrites revised figures in its current files. Only the PDF archive and ALFRED keep the numbers as first published.

**Assessment: No Known Issue (close to Moderate).** No files or data fields have been removed. The revisions are documented and follow normal statistical practice, and earlier versions are still available. The 2025 redefinition still means older and newer copies are not comparable, so preservationists should keep copies made before and after April 2025.

### 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- **Fall 2025 shutdown:** the 43-day lapse pushed September 2025 data from Oct 16 to Nov 25, 2025. Releases stayed compressed until the May 14, 2026 release. ([Census release schedule](https://www.census.gov/retail/release_schedule.html); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-census-bureau-release-sept-retail-sales-durable-goods-orders-reports-next-2025-11-19/))
- **Early 2026 lapse:** the January 2026 report came out Mar 6, 2026, with "Next release: To be determined." ([adv2601.pdf](https://www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/adv2601.pdf))
- **Annual revision delayed:** it normally comes out in April but was pushed to Sept 28, 2026. Census cited the move to AIES. ([adv2603.pdf](https://www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/adv2603.pdf); [2026 revision introduction](https://www.census.gov/retail/mrts/www/benchmark/2026/pdf/Introduction.pdf))
- **Related reports skipped (not MARTS itself):** the Advance Economic Indicators reports for Sep–Nov 2025 and Jan–Feb 2026 were dropped. ([Census](https://www.census.gov/econ/indicators/historical_data.html))
- **Current funding is temporary:** a continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103) runs only through Dec 11, 2026, so another lapse is possible.

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- **ICR renewed on time:** OMB control no. 0607-0717 ("Monthly Retail Surveys"), ICR 202511-0607-002, was approved Apr 6, 2026, before the Apr 30, 2026 expiration. The new expiration is Apr 30, 2029. ([reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202511-0607-002); Federal Register notices [90 FR 37468](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/05/2025-14783/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for) and [90 FR 55717](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/03/2025-21844/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for))
- **No month skipped:** every MARTS month was eventually published.
- **Back on schedule:** August 2026 data came out on time Sept 16, 2026, and the 2027 calendar is posted.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Normal release dates were missed for about six months, and the annual revision was about five months late. Nothing was skipped, the ICR is current, and releases are on schedule now.

### 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- **Timeliness:** it fell for several months in 2025–26 and has since been restored.
- **Response rate:** MARTS is voluntary, and the larger survey it draws from has a response rate of only about 63.7% for sales ([2026 revision introduction](https://www.census.gov/retail/mrts/www/benchmark/2026/pdf/Introduction.pdf)).
- **Smaller sample:** it was cut to about 4,800 firms in 2022 (before 2025).
- **Narrower coverage:** nonemployers were excluded starting April 2025.
- **Paper forms:** paper collection is being phased out starting late 2025 (90 FR 37468).
- **Strain on sister programs:** Census froze revisions to a sister survey's figures for 2026 "due to schedule and resource constraints" ([MTIS Jan 2026](https://www2.census.gov/mtis/historical/mtis2601.pdf)). This is not MARTS, but it suggests strain in the same economic directorate.
- **Field staff losses:** the Commerce Inspector General has reported shortages of survey field staff, and reporters have described losses in collection staff ([GovExec](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/07/census-has-long-struggled-staffing-shortages-employees-say-trump-making-it-worse/406840/)).

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- Industry detail, monthly frequency, error ranges and the 90% confidence intervals are all unchanged.
- The release lag has returned to its normal ~2 weeks.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** There has been no lasting cut in detail, frequency or timeliness. Risks are emerging from staffing, budget and response rates, and timeliness has been disrupted temporarily.

### 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for High or Moderate Risk**
- **Permissive authority:** Title 13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182 allow Census to run surveys but do not require MARTS by name or say what it must collect. Responses are voluntary.
- **Partial substitutes:** the full Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) gives the same figures about a month later. Private card-spending data (e.g., Visa SpendingPulse, Bank of America, the Chicago Fed's CARTS) cover part of the same ground.
- **"Non-mandated functions" language:** the FY2026 budget justification said Census would eliminate functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" ([Census Project](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/06/30/department-of-commerce-releases-fiscal-year-2026-census-budget-details/)).

**Evidence for No Known Issue or Moderate Risk**
- **Federal program use:** BEA uses it for GDP and the national accounts, as stated in the ICR abstract. The Federal Reserve, BLS and Treasury also use it.
- **Indicator status:** it is an OMB-designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator under Statistical Policy Directives 3 and 4.
- **No full substitute:** no other official, probability-based measure of spending is available at a two-week lag.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** No statute names MARTS specifically. GDP estimation and monetary policy rely on it, and the substitutes are only partial: MRTS is a month later and private data are not representative. The general authority and the "non-mandated" language keep this from being No Known Issue.

### 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk**
- **Staff losses:** Census lost about 1,300 staff by mid-2025 ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/census-bureau-doge-federal-surveys-fe560e377be69e913660a6d90c1ee419)) and about 1,500 by October 2025 to deferred resignation and similar programs ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/census-bureau-hit-with-layoffs-as-100-get-notices-in-shutdown)). The American Statistical Association estimates about 15% of staff lost since FY2024 ([ASA](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf)).
- **Layoff notices:** about 100 workers received layoff notices during the shutdown in October 2025.
- **Leadership:**
  - Director Santos resigned in February 2025.
  - In September 2025 the career acting director, Ron Jarmin, was replaced by George Cook, a political appointee who also holds Commerce's economic affairs undersecretary duties ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2025/09/19/nx-s1-5288846/trump-census-bureau-director-george-cook)).
  - Wikipedia, citing a social-media post, says Jarmin was deputy director only until May 2026; I could not confirm this from a second source.
  - AP reported 18 vacancies among top leaders in 2025.
- **Funding:**
  - FY2026 enacted gave the Current Surveys and Programs account $318.5M, $10M (about 3%) less than FY2025.
  - The FY2027 request is $288.5M, about 9.4% below FY2026. The House committee bill matches that figure ([CRS R48929](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48929); [CRS IF13105](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF13105.html)).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- The percentage of staff lost (~15%) and the size of the budget cuts (3–9%) fall in the Moderate or No Known Issue ranges.
- Total Census funding went up because of decennial census preparation.

**Note:** The USAJobs tracker you suggested could not be used. Its page did not load its figures in my check, and it says it was archived Dec 31, 2025.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The rubric's thresholds of 1,000 or more staff lost and leadership removed are both met. Budget cuts alone would be Moderate.

### 6. Policy

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- **Statistical agency merger:** the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets propose combining BLS, BEA and Census within Commerce, and the FY2027 Commerce request includes $600M for BLS ([CRS R48929](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48929); [DOL Talent Strategy](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/OPA/newsreleases/2025/08/Americas-Talent-Strategy-Building-the-Workforce-for-the-Golden-Age.pdf)).
- **Cutting "non-mandated" functions:** the FY2026 budget justification promised to eliminate functions that are not mandated by statute.
- **Data sharing:** a new notice (Oct 2, 2026) lets Census share data from its voluntary business surveys with BEA ([Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/02/2026-20249/notice-of-data-sharing-activity)).
- **Politicization concerns:** the BLS commissioner was fired in August 2025, and a political appointee now leads Census.

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- The ICR was filed as an "extension without change." OIRA recorded its decision as "approved with change," but I found nothing showing that change affected what MARTS collects.
- There is no Presidential Action–driven ICR and no negative policy note on the MARTS pages.
- Content changes (dropping nonemployers, moving to AIES) were planned before 2025 for technical reasons.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Changes to the agencies that produce this data have been proposed but not carried out. Nothing has directly changed what MARTS collects or publishes.

---

## Summary of risk levels
- Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**
- Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
- Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**
- Statutory Context: **Moderate Risk**
- Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**
- Policy: **Moderate Risk**
